newsitem.title: USA: USDA hopes to test meat inspection models in Oct.
newsitem.headline: USDA hopes to test meat inspection models in Oct.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department hopes to test new meat inspection models in slaughter plants "roughly in October," said Maggie Glavin, a top official at the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS).

FSIS is reassessing the tasks of government meat inspectors in the wake of a major overhaul of U.S. meat inspection rules that began last July. It was holding a one-and-a-half day meeting starting Tuesday to hear from industry and consumer groups.
FSIS is considering whether to redeploy inspectors from examining carcasses to new tasks in processing plants and during the distribution of meat and poultry products.

"The inspection procedures we currently use are based on a time when animal diseases were rampant and, thus, focus disproportionately on this area. And they do not mesh with our new regulatory approach..." said FSIS chief Thomas Billy in a written statement.

Meat industry groups were enthusiastic at Tuesday's session though some cautioned it might be too soon to tinker with the system since the industry is in the midst of implementing new rules based on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP).
"It's good to open the debate but we're not ready to move on all the fine points," said Rosemary Mucklow, executive director of the National Meat Association. "It's a little premature."
Representatives of the meat inspectors' union said FSIS should leave sight inspection in place, instead build on it.
"I think we need to continue to look at product as well as process if we truly want to protect the consumer," said Richard Wolff, president of the Northern Council of Food Inspection Locals.
Consumer groups said FSIS was jumping the gun.
"It's premature. It was our understanging that USDA would not do changes unless proven to be better than the current system," said Heather Klinkhammer of S.T.O.P, Safe Tables Our Priority.
Glavin emphasised the meeting was "the beginning of a very long process."
She said FSIS wanted to test new models in a total of nine pork, beef and poultry plants this fall and was seeking volunteers.
